rgb: The camera looks sharply downward over a narrow paved outdoor path, with a wall along the left side and dirt and vegetation on the right, as the wearer travels on a black bicycle. About 0.4 to 0.6 metres directly beneath and ahead of the wearer, and held by both hands, are the bicycle’s black handlebars, silver bell, frame, and front wheel; the wearer’s knees and blue shorts are partly visible along the bottom edge. Farther ahead on the right is a second, red bicycle carrying two people less than half a metre apart: a front cyclist wearing a white patterned dress and holding the handlebars, plus a rear passenger in blue pants and a white top sitting on the back carrier. During frames 1–3, this bicycle is approximately 2 to 3 metres ahead and right, oriented away from the camera in the same forward direction; only its rear wheel and the riders’ lower bodies appear at the upper-right edge because their upper bodies are cropped out. In frames 4 and 5, the camera wearer closes the gap and rides beside the red bicycle’s left side at 0.5 to 1 metre, placing it and its front rider within arm’s reach to the right, while turning the black handlebars slightly left. Both people on the red bicycle remain forward-facing, with their heads outside the top of the frame.
depth: The depth map presents a steeply downward egocentric perspective over a paved path, with a low wall to the left (~1–1.5 m away during frames 1–3). The camera wearer’s arms, knees, and bicycle handlebars form the brightest lower-foreground areas at ~0.3–0.8 m, within arm’s reach, while the road recedes downward and forward to ~1.5–3 m. Ahead on the right, a second bicycle carries a rider in blue pants and a passenger wearing a white dress; both face away from the wearer without looking back and are partly cut off by the top and right borders. From frame 1 through frame 5, the bicycles’ separation contracts from ~2.5–3 m in frame 1 to ~0.5–1 m when they are side by side on the wearer’s right in frame 5. As the wearer advances and veers slightly left, the other rider’s left arm holds their handlebar within arm’s reach of the wearer’s right hand, with ~0.4 m between them. Unlike RGB alone, the map clearly distinguishes the raised handlebars, Brake cables, and the approaching passenger’s dress and arm in 3D from the level roadway underneath. Nevertheless, depth is unreliable within the spoked wheels, where the visible ground behind the spokes receives inconsistent values, and in the upper background, where the flat road plane dissolves into uniform black.
segmentation: The segmentation output separates several distinct scene areas: the camera wearer’s left and right forearms and knees along the bottom (~0.3–0.8 m and within arm’s reach), the wearer’s bicycle frame and handlebars ahead (~0.6–1.2 m), and the second bicycle with its riders on the right as the wearer passes them, moving from ~2.5–3 m ahead in frame 1 to ~0.5–1 m to the right by frame 5. The wearer and the cyclists on the other bicycle all look forward along the direction of travel, away from the camera. Most of the other riders’ upper bodies remain beyond the top-right boundary until frame 5, when the passenger’s left arm extends forward to grasp that bicycle’s handlebar ~0.4 m from the wearer’s right hand. In frames 4 and 5, the masks help separate the approaching bicycle’s front wheel, the passenger’s skirt, and the wearer’s right arm. However, the steep overhead viewpoint makes both class assignments and instance borders highly unreliable. The wearer’s bicycle is entirely absent in frames 1 and 2, then wrongly labelled as ‘scissors’ in frame 3, ‘person’ with a green mask in frame 4, and ‘motorcycle’ with a purple mask in frame 5. The wearer’s knee is also incorrectly tagged as ‘carrot’ in frame 4, while multiple limbs and wheels are omitted or broken into fragments throughout the sequence.
pose: Across the five frames, the pose visualization is nearly empty: it finds no yellow full-body skeletons and only three separate magenta hand skeletons associated with the camera wearer’s handlebar grips, located ~0.5–0.7 m in front of the chest and within arm’s reach. More precisely, it detects the wearer’s left hand holding the left grip in frame 1, the right hand on the right grip in frame 3, and that right hand once more in frame 4 while the handlebars turn left. Where detection succeeds, the 2D wrist and finger landmarks clearly reveal the wearer’s curled gripping pose, with the thumb and fingers wrapped around the handlebar and brake lever—details that can be difficult to see in RGB because dark skin tones blend with the black grips. Even so, extreme self-occlusion and cropping caused by the sharply downward viewpoint make the estimator seriously unreliable for global spatial arrangement and tracking several people. It entirely fails to detect the wearer’s arms and legs, the left hand throughout frames 2–5, the right hand in frames 1, 2, and 5, and all bodies and hands of the nearby cyclists positioned ~0.5–3 m away on the right.
